paras: The hanging of Ben Holton was a night attack in March 1882 in Oldham County, Kentucky, in which John and Alexander Duncan, wealthy distillers, hanged Holton, a Black man, by the neck three times to make him confess to burning their barn. Holton survived, and the attack became public only when he sued the brothers for $50,000 in the United States court at Louisville in July 1882. Papers across the country carried the suit as a curiosity, and in October Holton settled it for $700.

According to a Louisville dispatch of July 27, a barn belonging to the Duncans burned one night in March, and Holton was the only man in the neighborhood who did not offer to help put out the flames. The Duncans charged him with setting the fire, and a detective they hired from Cincinnati gave up the case, "satisfied that Holton was innocent." A later Louisville dispatch said the brothers' property "had been repeatedly fired."

On a cold night the Duncans roused Holton from his bed, where he was sleeping with his family, and took him to their still-house to make him confess. When he denied the crime, they tied a rope about his neck and drew him up until he was unconscious, then repeated the hanging twice more as he went on refusing to confess. He "only missed death by a hair's breadth" the third time, was let down to the floor and left alone, and was confined to his bed for days afterward.
The detective, who had not known of the hanging at the time, testified that the Duncans had often suggested hanging and that he thought he had talked them out of it.

Fearing further violence, Holton left his home; the July dispatch said he left the state and sued as a non-resident, while the October dispatch said he came to Louisville and had the Duncans arrested. He filed his $50,000 suit on July 27, and the July dispatch said the Duncans would be arrested the next morning. By October 20 Holton had compromised the suit for $700, and no report of a criminal trial of the Duncans was found.

The story reached the press through the lawsuit, and the July 27 Louisville dispatch ran within days in Washington, Alexandria and Lancaster papers under heads such as "Suit for Hanging." A version credited to the Louisville Courier-Journal, headed "Damages for Being Hanged," travelled west to Nevada, Seattle and Astoria into September. Some headlines took Holton's side, with the Lancaster Intelligencer writing of a man hanged to confess "a Crime He Knew Nothing Of" and the Somerset Herald heading the dispatch "The Colored Man's Wrongs."

Other papers treated it lightly, as when the West Virginia Freeman remarked that the claim was "reasonable" because "We wouldn't be hung for that amount." The Waco Daily Examiner wrote that the Duncans had made themselves "executioners to Judge Lynch," while calling Holton "the gentleman of ebony hue" and "the darkey." The settlement was reported in October in Wheeling, St. Paul and Maysville, Kentucky, where the Wheeling Intelligencer headed it "Made Them Sweat."

The Waco Daily Examiner gave a different account, saying the Duncans lived in Louisville and acted from "a deep rooted dislike," not over the barn. In that version they hanged Holton from a tree at his own residence and went home, and another Black man who had watched from a distance cut him down and revived him. The Louisville dispatches, closer to the source, place the hanging in the still-house and say nothing of a rescuer.

reader.title: Hanging of Ben Holton
bases: Two named brothers seized a Black man at night over a suspected barn burning and hanged him by the neck repeatedly to force a confession; he survived and sued (A1, A8, A14).

Holton survived the hanging and later sued (A1, A14), and the papers name only two attackers, John and Alexander Duncan (A1, A5); the attack was extralegal and framed as forcing a confession to arson, and the Waco paper called the brothers 'executioners to Judge Lynch' (A5).

The July 27 Louisville dispatch (A1), the Courier-Journal account (A8), a separate Texas version (A5) and an October 20 Louisville dispatch (A14) all report that the Duncans hanged Holton by the neck and that he sued, though they differ on details.

accounts.label: Waco Daily Examiner
accounts.gist: The Duncans of Louisville, out of 'a deep rooted dislike', resolved to kill Holton, hanged him from a tree at his residence and went home; another Black man cut him down and revived him.

accounts.label: Louisville dispatch of October 20
accounts.gist: The Duncans' property had been repeatedly fired; they pulled Holton up by a rope several times to force a confession, he fled to Louisville, had them arrested, and settled his suit for $700.

framing.detail: Most papers ran the Louisville dispatch as an oddity under heads such as 'Suit for Hanging' and 'A Curious Case', repeating that a detective thought Holton innocent.
The Lancaster Intelligencer headlined 'Hanging a Negro Three Times to Make Him Confess a Crime He Knew Nothing Of' and the Somerset Herald 'The Colored Man's Wrongs.'
The Waco Daily Examiner wrote of the Duncans as 'executioners to Judge Lynch' while calling Holton 'the gentleman of ebony hue' and 'the darkey.'
The West Virginia Freeman joked that the $50,000 claim was 'reasonable'; the Wheeling Intelligencer headed the settlement 'Made Them Sweat.'
